reference.source: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: Typically evolves through a viral-like prodrome into a florid psychiatric phase (agitation, delusions, disorganised behaviour) that frequently reaches psychiatry before neurology
The mature syndrome combines seizures, orofacial and limb dyskinesias, mutism, memory failure, a reduced level of consciousness, and autonomic instability
Autonomic dysfunction (labile blood pressure, cardiac arrhythmia, hyperthermia, central hypoventilation) is a leading cause of intensive-care need and death
Antibodies target the GluN1 subunit of the NMDA receptor; diagnosis rests on detecting these antibodies, with cerebrospinal fluid testing more sensitive and specific than serum
An ovarian teratoma is a common trigger in young women, so pelvic imaging and tumour screening are mandatory even when the initial scan is unremarkable
MRI is often normal or only subtly abnormal, so a normal scan must not dissuade from the diagnosis in a compatible clinical picture

Management combines tumour removal where a teratoma is found with first-line immunotherapy (corticosteroids, intravenous immunoglobulin, plasma exchange) and escalation to second-line agents such as rituximab or cyclophosphamide
Recovery is often slow and stepwise over many months, typically reversing the order in which deficits appeared
reference.pathophysiology: The disorder is driven by immunoglobulin G antibodies against the GluN1 subunit of the N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor. Antibody binding causes reversible cross-linking and internalisation of surface receptors, reducing NMDA-mediated synaptic transmission particularly across frontostriatal and limbic circuits, which is thought to underlie the psychiatric, movement, and memory features. Because the mechanism is functional receptor loss rather than fixed neuronal destruction, deficits are potentially reversible once antibody production is suppressed. In a substantial proportion of young women the immune response is triggered by neural tissue within an ovarian teratoma, while other cases follow herpes simplex encephalitis or arise without an identified trigger.
additionalDifferentials: Primary psychiatric illness such as a first psychotic episode or catatonia
Viral (including herpes simplex) or other infective encephalitis
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome or serotonin syndrome
Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease and other rapidly progressive encephalopathies
additionalInvestigations: Cerebrospinal fluid analysis for lymphocytic pleocytosis, oligoclonal bands, and paired serum/CSF NMDA receptor antibodies
Electroencephalography, which may show the extreme delta brush pattern or diffuse slowing
MRI of the brain with contrast to exclude alternative structural or inflammatory causes
Pelvic and abdominal imaging (ultrasound, MRI or CT) to search for an ovarian teratoma
Whole-body tumour screening in older patients or when teratoma is not found
Screening for herpes simplex virus, which can precede antibody-mediated relapse
redFlags: Autonomic instability with cardiac arrhythmia, blood-pressure swings, or central hypoventilation requiring critical care
Rapidly declining consciousness and the need for airway protection
New or recurrent psychiatric decompensation after apparent recovery, suggesting relapse or an undetected tumour
reference.prognosis: Most patients improve substantially with tumour removal and immunotherapy, though recovery frequently takes many months and cognitive or behavioural sequelae may persist. Early treatment and identification of an associated teratoma are associated with better outcomes, while relapses occur in a minority and warrant repeat tumour surveillance.
pitfalls: Attributing the presentation to a primary psychiatric disorder and delaying immunological investigation
Excluding the diagnosis because MRI is normal
Testing serum alone and missing antibodies detectable only in cerebrospinal fluid
Failing to search repeatedly for an ovarian teratoma when the first imaging is negative
Prematurely stopping escalation of therapy in patients who respond slowly
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
